sections.html:
Up in New Mexico's northwest, on the Arizona border, McKinley County has just one incorporated city, Gallup, which is also the seat. The 2020 census counted 72,902 residents, with 21,899 in Gallup and 2,900 in Crownpoint. That leaves 48,103 people spread across rural communities such as Thoreau, Tohatchi, Church Rock, Ramah, Pinehaven and Zuni Pueblo.

Over 60 percent of the county's land is part of the Navajo Nation or the Zuni Reservation. Median home value is $72,100, well under the state midpoint, so bills run smaller in dollars, though penalties work as they do elsewhere in the state. For most parcels, step one is learning which jurisdiction the land falls under.

sections.h2: Fee land, trust land and what you can sell
sections.html:
Land status decides which rules apply. Trust land inside the reservations is not subject to state or local taxes, though tribes may tax it to fund their own services. The Navajo Nation also levies a possessory interest tax on the right to use Navajo land for something like an oil and gas lease, a right-of-way or a business site lease. Fee land, ordinary privately owned land with a deed, stays under county rules.

  • Fee land with a recorded deed is assessed by the McKinley County Assessor and billed by the Treasurer.
  • Trust land and tribal land assignments follow tribal and federal procedures.
  • Before you price or advertise, find out whether your land is fee, trust, or held by lease or assignment.

The assessor's records and the county clerk's recorded documents are the quickest way to tell fee land from other holdings. A title company will ask the same thing first.

The McKinley County Assessor lists and values taxable property. The McKinley County Treasurer collects taxes, penalties and interest under the Property Tax Code, Sections 7-35-1 through 7-38-90 NMSA 1978.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it
County TreasurerCollects property tax, manages county funds207 W Hill Ave, Suite 101, Gallup, NM 87301; (505) 722-4459; open 8 AM to 5 PM on weekdays
County AssessorDiscovers, lists and inventories taxable propertyAssessor page on the county site
Treasurer web portalAccount lookup by property tax account numberOnline

The county posts charts of taxes billed by taxing entity for each tax year, which show how one bill divides among county, school and other districts. The county's treasurer and assessor pages are the place to begin.

McKinley County follows the statewide calendar, with payments due November 10 and April 10.

  • January 1: value is set for the year, and the tax lien attaches.
  • September 1: state finance officials set the rates.
  • November 1: bills go out.
  • November 10: first half due. Interest begins after December 10.
  • April 10: second half due. Interest begins after May 10.
  • January 10 of the next year: final day for a refund claim in district court.

Interest on late payments is 1 percent a month. Section 7-38-48 makes the tax a first lien that outranks every other interest, so an unpaid McKinley County bill stays with the house and lands on the next owner.

As of January 1, the assessor puts a current and correct value on your home, and one third of that is taxable. A residential assessment may climb no more than 3 percent a year, unless ownership changes or the property is improved or rezoned.

Two things change at a sale. The cap lifts, so the buyer starts with a fresh valuation. The $2,000 head of family exemption, which covers a resident's primary home, is removed. Passing the home to a child who lives there, or into a revocable trust for a spouse or child, is not treated as a change of ownership.

sections.h2: How to appeal a high valuation
sections.html:
Your written petition must reach the assessor by April 1 or 30 days after the notice of valuation is mailed, whichever is later. The county valuation protest board decides it, and the state's Appraisal Bureau supplies one member.

A protest filed on time shields the disputed portion from delinquency. The other option is paying first and seeking a refund in district court. An initial protest costs nothing, and the state department publishes a protest pamphlet.

Once three full years go by without payment, the account passes to the state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau, which may sell the property at public auction. First it tries phone calls, certified mail, visits and notices left at the property, and it offers installment agreements.

Any auction proceeds beyond the tax, penalty, interest and costs go back to the former owner. Each county must have an auction every year, McKinley included.

  • Heirs of a house on fee land should review the treasurer's account first thing.
  • Owners who have moved away should make sure the treasurer holds a current mailing address.

sections.h2: How a quick sale usually goes
sections.html:
You show ownership, clear any tax lien and sign a deed, which the county clerk records. Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978 says an unrecorded deed has no effect on title against a later purchaser, and recording is how the buyer is protected.

When the house belongs to an estate, probate goes first. Real property rules out the small-estate affidavit, and a personal representative's deed may be what moves title from the decedent.

A sensible order is to confirm the land is fee land, get the treasurer's payoff, finish any probate step, then sign and record. A cash buyer closing as-is typically takes care of the rest. Before any of that, collect your deed, the latest tax bill and, for an inherited house, the estate papers, since the title company starts with those.

sections.h2: Timing a McKinley County sale around the tax year
sections.html:
When you sell matters less than whether the taxes are settled, but the calendar still shapes the paperwork. A sale in the spring, after the April 10 installment, usually means the current year is half paid. A sale in autumn may close before the bill even exists, since bills are mailed November 1.

Because the January 1 lien attaches no matter who owns the house later, buyers and title companies look at two numbers: what is owed from past years and what is owed for this one. Ask the treasurer for both, in writing if you can, and keep the answer with your closing papers.

If you are selling a rural home, ask the county clerk's office what is on record against it. A recorded deed, a clear chain of ownership and a paid-up treasurer's account are the three things a buyer will check. Owners of manufactured homes should also ask the assessor about the release before they list, since the home cannot be moved or retitled without one.

Finally, remember that the notice of valuation is not the bill. It arrives in spring, the bill arrives in November, and an unopened envelope in either month is the usual way a deadline is missed.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in McKinley County, NM?
faqs.a: The McKinley County Treasurer, 207 W Hill Ave, Suite 101, Gallup, (505) 722-4459, open weekdays 8 AM to 5 PM.

faqs.q: When are McKinley County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 10 and the second April 10, with interest starting after December 10 and May 10.

faqs.q: Is trust land in McKinley County taxed by the county?
faqs.a: No. Trust land is not subject to state or local taxes. Tribes may assess their own taxes, such as the Navajo possessory interest tax.

faqs.q: How long do I have to protest my valuation?
faqs.a: The later of 30 days after the assessor mails the notice or April 1. The petition goes to the county assessor.

faqs.q: Can I sell a McKinley County house that has delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Because the lien outranks other interests, the tax must be paid or settled at closing. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure.
